design_detail: Review of records in the California Poison Control System (CPCS) database, a 24-hour emergency telephone consultation service, for calls coded ecstasy, MDMA, methylenedioxymethamphetamine or XTC from 1 January 2000 to 9 October 2005. The paper labels the design three ways: a retrospective review (abstract), a 'nonconcurrent, prospective, observational case series' (Methods, p. 165) and a 'retrospective observational case series' (Limitations, p. 168). CPCS staff recorded what the treating hospital reported by telephone; no hospital records were obtained. Two authors reviewed every case; three authors abstracted, on a standard form, the cases with a documented sodium (a number or 'normal') and all cases with a seizure. Women and men were compared with univariate logistic regression, and for sodium values below 130 mmol/L with a Wilcoxon test and a mean difference (pp. 165-167).
can_establish: What 545 reported ecstasy-related poisoning calls to one poison-control system looked like; how many of the 188 with a recorded sodium had a level below 130 mmol/L (73), how women and men compared among those 188, and what happened to the people with low sodium (seizure, coma, intensive care, death), including the 4 deaths among them.
cannot_establish: How common low sodium is among people who take MDMA (the denominator is calls to a poison-control system, and a sodium level was recorded for only about a third); whether women are more likely than men to develop it (testing was not random, no adjustment was made, and fluid, weight, kidney function and the amount of MDMA are not reported); whether MDMA caused each case (no gas-chromatography confirmation, and 35 of 103 people with a drug screen were negative for amphetamines); the part played by fluid, heat or dancing (not recorded); or whether sex changes how low sodium affects coma or seizure (no interaction test, and the intervals for women and men overlap).

sample.recruitment: All records in the CPCS database coded as ecstasy, MDMA, methylenedioxymethamphetamine or XTC (by code or free text), 1 January 2000 to 9 October 2005: 1,436 cases after duplicates were removed. Excluded: 267 managed at home; 616 by outcome code (29 'no effect', 63 'unrelated', 2 'confirmed non-exposure', 3 'judged nontoxic', 167 'minimal clinical effects possible', 352 'unable to follow - potentially toxic'); 5 on manual review with no MDMA exposure (miscoded); 3 with no sex recorded. 545 were included (Methods, pp. 165-166; Results, p. 166; Figure 1, p. 167).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Any ecstasy exposure with an outcome known and some effect; information-only calls and cases managed at home excluded; co-ingestions allowed; no age limit (Methods, pp. 165-166).
sample.demographics: 296 women (54.3%) and 249 men (45.7%); mean age 21.2 years (SD 6.8); the same mean and SD (21.2, 6.76) are printed for women and for men in Table 1 (p. 167).
sample.attrition: 357 of 545 (65.5%) had no documented sodium; of the 188 that did, 134 had a number and 54 were recorded only as 'normal' (Results, p. 166; Limitations, p. 169).
sample.selection_effects: Voluntary calls from hospitals and the public, so a passive surveillance source. A sodium was recorded for 35% of women and 33% of men, so the comparison of women and men is among those a clinician chose to test. The authors say referral bias may make the series represent the more severe cases (Limitations, pp. 168-169).

exposure.measurement: History of use as recorded by CPCS staff. A urine drug screen was documented in 103 of the 188 people with a recorded sodium (68 positive and 35 negative for amphetamines or derivatives); the type of assay was not recorded; no gas chromatography-mass spectrometry was reported; the 35 negative cases were counted as MDMA cases from the history (Results, p. 166; Limitations, p. 169).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported: the amount of MDMA and the amount of fluid drunk are not given. 'Rave party' is recorded as the site of use for 50 of 545 (9.1%), including 3 of the 74 low-sodium cases (4.1%) (Results, p. 166).
exposure.polysubstance: Co-ingestion was allowed. Of 103 urine screens, 35 (34%) were also positive for another drug, most often cocaine, tetrahydrocannabinol and benzodiazepines (Results, p. 166).

comparison.controls: Within the 188 with a recorded sodium: women against men for sodium below 130 mmol/L (55 of 105 against 18 of 83); and, within each sex, people with low sodium against those without (55 against 50 women; 18 against 65 men) for seizure, coma, tachycardia, agitation, hyperthermia and death (Results, pp. 167-168; Tables 2 and 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Body size, kidney function, hydration and fluid intake, amount of MDMA, time since use, heat and exertion, other drugs. The authors list body habitus, renal function, hydration, co-ingestions and behavioural factors (Limitations, p. 169).

outcomes.instruments: Serum sodium as measured at the referring hospital and relayed by telephone; seizure, tachycardia, agitation, hyperthermia, coma, intensive care admission and death from the CPCS record (codes and free text).
outcomes.validity_norms: Low sodium is defined as below 130 mmol/L; hyperthermia, coma and seizure are not defined; no attempt was made to confirm sodium values from hospital records (Methods of Measurement, p. 166).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary outcome: sodium below 130 mmol/L among people with an ecstasy exposure and a documented sodium. Secondary: seizures, tachycardia, agitation, hyperthermia, coma and death among those with a documented sodium (Outcome Measures, p. 166).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 13 odds ratios are reported (1 for sex and low sodium; 6 outcomes in each sex), plus a Wilcoxon test of sodium values; formal tests were limited to the a priori sex hypothesis (Primary Data Analysis, p. 166).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None; two authors reviewed each case and three abstracted the detailed cases, with disagreements settled by discussion and inter-rater reliability not formally tested (Data Collection, p. 166).

analysis.effect_sizes: Of 545: 296 women, 249 men. Documented sodium in 188 (34.5%); sodium below 130 mmol/L in 73 (abstract, Table 2), 55 of 105 women (52.4%) and 18 of 83 men (21.7%); odds ratio for female sex 3.97 (95% CI 2.08-7.59). Median sodium among those with low sodium 122 mmol/L (25th-75th percentile 119-124). Within each sex, low sodium against none, odds ratios: coma women 3.93 (1.20-12.90), men 0.78 (0.15-3.97); seizure women 4.38 (1.74-11.00), men 2.21 (0.69-7.07); tachycardia women 0.33 (0.14-0.81), men 0.13 (0.04-0.51); agitation women 0.41 (0.17-0.98), men 1.3 (0.43-4.00); hyperthermia women 0.58 (0.15-2.17), men 0.29 (0.04-2.40); death women 1.39 (0.22-8.65), men 1.85 (0.16-21.70). Deaths 13 of 545 (2.4%), 4 among the people with low sodium (3 women, 1 man), all 4 with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing drugs to support it. Among all 545: tachycardia 43%, agitation 32%, seizure 11%, hyperthermia 40 (7.3%), intensive care 153 (28%).
analysis.selective_reporting: The sex hypothesis is described as a priori. All six secondary outcomes are reported in both sexes. The Discussion stresses the coma and seizure odds ratios in women, although their intervals overlap those in men and no test of a difference is given.
analysis.power: No power calculation. Several cells are small, for example 4 deaths among the 73 with low sodium, giving very wide intervals (death in men 1.85, 0.16-21.70).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 188 people with a recorded sodium after a reported ecstasy exposure, 73 had a level below 130 mmol/L, 55 of 105 women (about 52 in 100) and 18 of 83 men (about 22 in 100); the odds of low sodium were about four times higher in women (3.97, 2.08-7.59). Among women, those with low sodium had higher odds of coma and seizure than those without (3.93 and 4.38); among men the intervals included no difference (0.78 and 2.21), but the intervals for women and men overlap. 4 of the 73 with low sodium died, all with brain swelling on CT. Everything is unadjusted and rests on a third of cases having a sodium recorded.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says female sex was associated with increased odds of low sodium and of low-sodium-associated coma, and that confounders prevent any statement about cause. The Editor's Capsule says women were 'four times more likely' (52 in 100 against 22 in 100 is about 2.4 times; the 4 is an odds ratio), and the Discussion says the study 'provides support that such a sex difference does indeed exist' and that the pattern could fit sex acting as an effect modifier, which no interaction test examines.

timeline.event: Low sodium with catatonic stupor after ecstasy (Maxwell and colleagues; reference 18 of this paper).
Near-fatal coma with raised vasopressin after ecstasy (Holden and Jackson; reference 20), as cited by this paper.
Rise in vasopressin with a fall in sodium in healthy, normally hydrated men given MDMA (Henry and colleagues; reference 25), as cited by this paper; not read here.
28-month series of 17 people from a UK poisons service, 10 of them women, 2 deaths (both women).

Series of 18 people with low sodium after ecstasy, 17 of them women (Budisavljevic and colleagues), and a 3-month Israeli series of 32 emergency patients with 3 low-sodium cases, 2 of them women (Ben-Abraham and colleagues), both as cited by this paper; not read here.
This review: 545 California poison-centre reports, 73 with a recorded low sodium, 4 deaths among them.
Narrative review that tabulates published cases of low sodium after ecstasy, including rows from this series.

replication.where_it_stands: Low sodium after MDMA with seizures and brain swelling has been seen in poison-centre and hospital series on two continents and in many case reports. All are selected reports of people who became ill; none compares people who drank a large amount with people who did not. The sex difference rests on this one study (among people who were tested) and on the mostly female make-up of case reports (17 of 18 in one earlier series, 10 of 17 in another), which reflects who was reported rather than who is at risk.

funding.funder: No funder for the study is stated. One author (Blanc) was supported in part by a National Institute on Drug Abuse grant (DA 14935).
funding.affiliations_note: Emergency physicians and toxicologists at California hospitals and universities; several authors work for the California Poison Control System, whose records are analysed.

what_would_settle_it: A sodium measured on arrival in every person presenting after MDMA (not only those a clinician chose to test), with laboratory-confirmed MDMA, recorded fluid intake, body weight, time since use and setting, and an analysis adjusted for these that tests whether sex changes the link between low sodium and coma or seizure.

domains.note: Univariate analysis only; no fluid intake, MDMA amount, body size, kidney function, heat or exertion, so women and men (and people with and without low sodium) differ in unmeasured ways.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Voluntary calls; a sodium was recorded for only 34.5%, and who was tested is not random; 352 potentially toxic cases 'unable to follow' were set aside.
MDMA exposure by history; urine screen in 103 of 188, 35 negative for amphetamines and still counted; no confirmatory assay.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Not a trial; treatment not the subject.
No sodium recorded for 65.5% of cases; 54 of the 188 recorded only as 'normal'; timing of the sodium not consistent.
Sodium values relayed by telephone and never checked against hospital records; coma, seizure and hyperthermia not defined.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Sex hypothesis stated in advance and all secondary outcomes shown, but the interpretation leans on the women-only coma and seizure odds ratios and the text and tables disagree on several counts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A retrospective, unadjusted analysis of voluntary telephone reports, appraised with ROBINS-I as the library does for other case series. Cite it for what these 545 reports and the 73 low-sodium cases looked like and for the unadjusted women-against-men counts among those tested; do not cite it for how common low sodium is, for risk by sex, or for cause.

key_findings.finding: Source and method: the CPCS is a 24-hour emergency telephone service; staff recorded what callers reported; sodium levels were measured at the referring hospitals and recorded as reported by telephone, with no attempt to confirm them from hospital records; two authors reviewed each case and three abstracted the cases with a sodium (numeric or 'normal') and all cases with a seizure; inter-rater reliability was not formally tested.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 'Study Design and Setting', 'Data Collection and Processing', 'Methods of Measurement'

key_findings.finding: Selection: 1,436 cases identified; 545 included after excluding 267 managed at home, 616 by outcome code, 5 miscoded and 3 without sex. A serum sodium was documented in 188 (34.5%): 105 of 296 women (35%) and 83 of 249 men (33%); 134 as a number and 54 as 'normal'. 357 (65.5%) had no sodium recorded.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph and 'Characteristics of Study Subjects' (p. 166); Figure 1 (p. 167)

key_findings.finding: Main comparison among the 188: sodium below 130 mmol/L in 73, 55 of 105 women (52.4%) and 18 of 83 men (21.7%); odds ratio for female sex 3.97 (95% CI 2.08-7.59). Among the 115 without low sodium, 50 were women and 65 men. The median sodium among those with low sodium was 122 mmol/L (25th-75th percentile 119-124).

Within each sex, low sodium against none (unadjusted odds ratios, Table 3): coma women 3.93 (1.20-12.90), men 0.78 (0.15-3.97); seizure women 4.38 (1.74-11.00), men 2.21 (0.69-7.07); tachycardia women 0.33 (0.14-0.81), men 0.13 (0.04-0.51); agitation women 0.41 (0.17-0.98), men 1.3 (0.43-4.00); hyperthermia women 0.58 (0.15-2.17), men 0.29 (0.04-2.40); death women 1.39 (0.22-8.65), men 1.85 (0.16-21.70). Low sodium was linked to lower odds of tachycardia in both sexes; the authors call the reason unclear.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and the paragraph below it; Discussion, last paragraph (p. 171)

key_findings.finding: Deaths: 13 of 545 (2.4%). 4 occurred among the people with low sodium (3 women, 1 man): all had a urine test positive for amphetamines or derivatives (1 specifically for MDMA), low blood pressure needing drugs to support it, and brain swelling confirmed by CT; 2 had seizures, 1 presented with a body temperature of 34.4 degrees Celsius and 2 had fluid on the lungs. Of the 9 deaths without low sodium (6 women, 3 men): 5 had asystole or ventricular fibrillation, 3 hyperthermia, 1 severe acidosis with brain death and 2 fatal bleeding in the head (categories overlap).
key_findings.locator: Results, last two paragraphs (left and right columns)

key_findings.finding: Among all 545: tachycardia 232 (42.6%), agitation 174 (31.9%), coma 54 (9.9%), seizure 61 (11.2%), hyperthermia 40 (7.3%; women 16, men 24), intensive care 153 (28.1%), death 13 (2.4%). 'Rave party' was recorded as the site of use for 50 (9.1%), including 3 of the 74 low-sodium cases (4.1%).

MDMA confirmation: urine drug screening was documented in 103 of the 188 (54.8%); 68 positive and 35 (34%) negative for amphetamines or derivatives, and the 35 were still counted as MDMA cases from the history; 35 were also positive for another drug (cocaine, THC and benzodiazepines most often). Among the 73 with low sodium, 43 had a drug screen, 39 positive and 4 negative. No gas chromatography-mass spectrometry was reported and the assay type was not recorded. The paper reports neither the amount of MDMA nor fluid intake.

The authors' own limits: passive surveillance subject to reporting bias; telephone-recorded data; referral bias that may make the series represent more severe cases; MDMA unconfirmed in a large share; no sodium in 65.5% of cases; timing of the sodium not consistent; low sodium may be a mild, self-correcting process in some people; and confounders (body habitus, kidney function, hydration, co-ingestions, behaviour) prevent attributing cause.

Discussion, as hypotheses: sex hormones (estrogen) may shape vasopressin release and the brain's response to low sodium; cited evidence is from rats, from postoperative patients, from a 1998 letter on vasopressin in eight healthy men and from case reports, all second-hand. The authors say women were no more or less likely to have a sodium test (35% against 33%) and that confounders preclude any definitive statement on the nature and mechanisms of the sex difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The count of low-sodium cases differs: 73 (38.8% of 188) in the abstract, Table 2 and Table 3, against 74 (39.4%) in the Results text, and '3 of the 74' for the rave-party figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use 73, which agrees with the sex counts (55 + 18) and the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Women's share of the 545 is 54.3% in the abstract and Table 1 but 54.6% (and men 45.4%) in the text; 296 of 545 is 54.3%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small printing error in the text.

reporting_issues.issue: Deaths by sex: Table 1 gives 8 women and 5 men (13 in all), but the Results text (3 women and 1 man with low sodium; 6 women and 3 men without) and the appendix list of the 13 deaths give 9 women and 4 men.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex split of the 13 deaths is uncertain; the paper's own sources disagree.

reporting_issues.issue: The odds ratio for seizure in men with low sodium is 2.11 in the text but 2.21 in Table 3; the confidence interval (0.69-7.07) is centred on 2.21.

The sentence giving medians of 124 mmol/L for women and 137 mmol/L for men (all quantified values, Figure 2) is followed by a Wilcoxon P of .77 and a mean sex difference of 0.07 mmol/L (-2.2 to 2.1). These cannot describe the same values; the Methods say the comparison was for values below 130 mmol/L.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence is unclear; the medians say nothing about the size of the fall in those with low sodium. Do not quote the two medians as a sex difference in sodium.

reporting_issues.issue: The Editor's Capsule says women were 4 times more likely to have low sodium. The proportions (about 52 in 100 against 22 in 100) give a ratio of about 2.4; the 4 is an odds ratio.
reporting_issues.consequence: Report the proportions first; do not describe the odds ratio as 'times more likely'.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list the outcome codes excluded but not 'unable to follow - potentially toxic', which the Results and Figure 1 show as the largest coded exclusion (352 of 1,436 cases, about one in four).
reporting_issues.consequence: A quarter of all calls were set aside by a rule not described in the Methods; whether they were more or less severe is not known.

reporting_issues.issue: The design is called a retrospective review in the abstract, a 'nonconcurrent, prospective, observational case series' in the Methods and a retrospective observational case series in the Limitations.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is a retrospective analysis of a database that was kept prospectively; no protocol or registration is described.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the pattern could be consistent with sex acting as an effect modifier, but no test of interaction is reported and the intervals for women and men overlap (coma 1.20-12.90 against 0.15-3.97).
reporting_issues.consequence: The finding that low sodium is linked to coma 'in women but not in men' is not shown as a difference between women and men.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the same mean age and SD (21.2, 6.76) for women and for men; coma, seizure, hyperthermia and tachycardia are not defined.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probable copying error in Table 1; outcome definitions cannot be checked.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 164-171.e1 (PDFs/MDMA/Rosenson_2007_HyponatremiaCalifornia.pdf), full text including Tables 1-3, Figures 1-2, Limitations, Discussion, references and Appendix E1. Tables 1-3 and the less-than sign in the sodium definition (lost in the text layer) were checked on renders; Appendix E1 was used only to check the sex of the 13 deaths and is not cited in any claim.
